Published 5 days ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (left) and Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan (right), pictured in a composite image as diplomatic tensions between the two countries escalate. Image: Kulu Media (Illustration) Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese consular staff members to leave the country within 48 hours, deepening a diplomatic dispute between the neighboring countries amid allegations involving Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. A senior Ethiopian official confirmed the departure order to Reuters in a report published on November 4, 2026. The six officials were stationed at Sudan’s consulate in Assosa, the capital of Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region near the Sudanese border. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, did not explain the reason for the decision. Ethiopia’s government had not publicly provided a detailed explanation of the move at the time of the Reuters report. The expulsion order comes amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum, with both governments accusing each other of involvement in armed conflicts affecting the wider Horn of Africa. Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing the RSF to use Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks against civilian infrastructure inside Sudan. Khartoum says it has submitted complaints to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over the alleged attacks. The latest accusations follow months of Ethiopia-Sudan tensions involving border security, drone operations and the wider Sudanese civil war. Sudanese military officials have previously alleged that RSF drones were being launched from Ethiopian territory, claims rejected by Addis Ababa. Ethiopia denies supporting the RSF. The allegations concerning the use of Ethiopian territory for drone operations have not been independently established. The diplomatic dispute has intensified as Sudan’s civil war continues and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises concerns about the security of the region’s shared borders. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused neighboring countries of supporting TPLF-aligned forces involved in renewed hostilities against the Ethiopian federal government. The accusations specifically concern Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt, all of which have denied supporting the armed groups. The competing allegations have heightened tensions between governments already facing significant security and diplomatic challenges. Assosa’s location gives the latest development particular significance. The town lies in western Ethiopia, close to Sudan, and serves as an important administrative center in a region affected by cross-border security concerns. Sudan’s consular presence there has provided a channel for official communication and assistance to Sudanese nationals. The departure of the six staff members could further complicate diplomatic engagement, although the immediate consequences for consular services remain unclear. The latest development follows a series of diplomatic confrontations involving Ethiopia and neighboring countries. On October 1, Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, accusing Asmara of activities threatening Ethiopian national security. Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia, while the two governments exchanged accusations over the renewed conflict in northern Ethiopia. The deterioration in relations coincided with reports of Eritrean military movements inside eastern Tigray and drone strikes reportedly targeting Eritrean forces. The reported incidents further increased concerns about a wider regional confrontation. The diplomatic dispute also extended to Egypt after Addis Ababa ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave the country and Cairo responded with a reciprocal measure. The African Union called for restraint and urged the governments involved to resolve their differences through diplomatic channels. The growing tensions have renewed concerns that separate conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan could become increasingly interconnected. Sudan’s civil war began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF. The conflict has caused widespread destruction, mass displacement and one of the world’s most severe humanitarian emergencies. According to Reuters, more than 14 million people have been displaced by the fighting. The war has also complicated relations with Sudan’s neighbors, particularly as rival parties accuse regional governments of providing military assistance or allowing armed groups to operate across borders. The regional security implications have become increasingly serious as Sudan’s conflict intersects with diplomatic rivalries involving Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt. Military movements near the Ethiopia-Sudan border and competing allegations of foreign support have added to concerns about wider instability. Eritrea has also accused Ethiopia of supporting Sudan’s RSF and destabilizing the Horn of Africa. Addis Ababa has denied supporting the paramilitary group, and the allegations have not been independently verified. In Ethiopia, the renewed confrontation involving federal forces and TPLF-aligned forces has raised fresh concerns about the durability of the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the major phase of the earlier Tigray war. The security situation in northern Ethiopia remains fragile. In October, reported drone strikes near Adigrat were followed by accounts of Eritrean troop movements, illustrating how the renewed conflict has affected relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Sudanese presidential adviser Amjad Farid said Khartoum was seeking to avoid an open war with Ethiopia despite the worsening diplomatic situation. Speaking to Reuters, Farid said Sudan remained committed to defending its territory while making efforts to prevent a direct military confrontation. The departure order for the six Sudanese consular staff members adds another layer of uncertainty to relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum. It remains unclear whether the measure will lead to further diplomatic restrictions, reciprocal expulsions or renewed negotiations between the two governments. With Sudan’s civil war continuing and security tensions rising across northern and western Ethiopia, the latest dispute underscores the risk that unresolved regional disagreements could further undermine stability across the Horn of Africa. Published 5 days ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk The US Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C. The department announced that Abraham Teklu Lemma pleaded guilty to transmitting classified intelligence to Ethiopian officials. Credit: APK / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 4.0 An Ethiopian-born American citizen who previously worked as a US government contractor has pleaded guilty to providing highly classified American intelligence to Ethiopian officials during a period that overlapped with the Tigray war, according to the US Department of Justice. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a Maryland resident who held a Top Secret security clearance, admitted on November 3, 2026, to conspiring to transmit US national defense information to the Ethiopian government. Prosecutors said the intelligence concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia and was supplied to senior officials within the country’s political, military and intelligence institutions. In an official announcement , the Justice Department said Lemma worked as an information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the US Department of State and the Department of Justice. According to court documents, Lemma collected and transmitted dozens of highly classified documents, notes, photographs and other materials between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023. Some of the information carried the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information classification, one of the highest levels of protection applied to US national security intelligence. Prosecutors said Lemma used his access as an IT administrator to retrieve classified information from government systems. He also copied sensitive information into handwritten notes and secretly carried them outside secure facilities. The Justice Department said these activities enabled him to pass restricted intelligence to Ethiopian government officials over an extended period. The case has drawn particular attention because the alleged espionage activities coincided with Ethiopia’s devastating northern conflict, which began in November 2020 and involved federal forces, TPLF-aligned forces and other armed actors. Although US authorities did not explicitly identify the conflict as the Tigray war in their November 3 announcement, the period covered by Lemma’s activities substantially overlaps with the fighting and its aftermath. The AFP report published on November 4 also noted the connection between the timeline of the intelligence disclosures and the conflict involving Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). US prosecutors said Lemma went beyond transmitting intelligence and, on some occasions, encouraged Ethiopian officials to take direct military action against armed groups opposing the federal government. In one exchange dated December 18, 2021, Lemma reportedly told an Ethiopian official that the opposing fighters had to be defeated to achieve peace. Later that day, according to the Justice Department, he transmitted additional information and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].” The reference to drones is particularly significant because unmanned aircraft were used during Ethiopia’s northern conflict. However, the department did not identify a specific drone operation resulting from that communication or publicly establish that a particular attack was carried out because of Lemma’s message. US officials also said the intelligence he provided was used in military operations. Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, stated that Ethiopian officials used classified national defense information supplied by Lemma during the conflict. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said Lemma had exploited his privileged access to remove sensitive information from secure facilities and transmit it to Ethiopian officials in the hope that it would help them target and kill opposing fighters. Read Ethiopia ranks 30th in Governance Index as security decline offsets gains By our staff reporter, Photo by Anteneh Aklilu November 8, 2026 Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Ethiopia ranks joint 30th among Africa’s 54 countries in the 2026 Ibrahim Index of African Governance, with improvements in economic opportunity and human development partly offset by a deterioration in security and the rule of law. The country scored 48.4 out of 100 for Overall Governance in 2025, below the continental average of 50.1 but above the East African average of 47.5. Its overall score improved by 1.8 points between 2016 and 2025, according to the Mo Ibrahim Foundation’s country profile. Despite that decade-long improvement, the foundation placed Ethiopia in its “Warning Signs” trend category. Ethiopia shares 30th place with Zimbabwe, which follows a different trajectory classified as “Increasing Improvement”. Released on October 31, the 2026 index assesses governance performance over the decade from 2016 to 2025 across four categories: Security & Rule of Law; Participation, Rights & Inclusion; Foundations for Economic Opportunity; and Human Development. Foundations for Economic Opportunity was Ethiopia’s strongest-performing category, scoring 54.5 out of 100 in 2025 after gaining 4.8 points over the decade. Human Development scored 53.6, an improvement of 1.8 points. Participation, Rights & Inclusion also improved over the full period, rising by 2.7 points to 41.5. It nevertheless remained Ethiopia’s lowest-scoring category. Security & Rule of Law moved in the opposite direction, falling by 2.4 points to 43.8. The decline constrained the country’s overall progress, illustrating the uneven performance behind its aggregate score. The findings distinguish between Ethiopia’s position in 2025 and its progress over the preceding decade: the country recorded a net improvement in Overall Governance, but its score remained below the African average and its trend carried the foundation’s warning classification. Within East Africa, Ethiopia ranked below Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda, which placed 10th, 14th, 18th and 28th respectively. It ranked above Djibouti in 35th place, Eritrea in 51st, Sudan in 52nd, Somalia in 53rd and South Sudan in 54th. The rankings also show that a country’s current position does not necessarily reflect the direction of its governance performance. South Sudan, despite ranking last, was classified as showing “Increasing Improvement”, while fifth-ranked South Africa was classified as experiencing “Increasing Deterioration”. Across Africa, the foundation reported slight improvement in Overall Governance over the decade, driven primarily by economic opportunity and human development. Foundations for Economic Opportunity improved in 44 countries, home to 68 per cent of the continent’s population. Infrastructure recorded the largest improvement among the index’s 16 subcategories, advancing in 52 countries—all except Nigeria and Gambia. The gains were led by mobile connectivity and improved access to energy and the internet. However, Security & Rule of Law deteriorated in 34 countries, while Participation, Rights & Inclusion declined in 31 countries. These countries account for 78 per cent and 60 per cent of Africa’s population respectively. Mo Ibrahim, the foundation’s founder and chair, warned that economic and social progress could not sustainably substitute for stronger institutions and security. “Economic and social gains will not last, and will anyway always be weaker, without progress in security, rule of law and participation,” he said. The index draws on 96 indicators using data from 51 African and international sources. This reflects our assessment of the security situation and reports of cross-border incidents affecting the Kenyan side of the border," the FCDO said. ‎The warning comes as Kenyan security agencies step up operations along the border following fighting that erupted on October 22 in neighbouring Ethiopia. ‎Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja on Thursday, November 5, ordered the deployment of additional officers to reinforce security in the border town. ‎During a security assessment visit, Kanja said officers had been directed to strengthen surveillance and remain on high alert to prevent the violence from spilling further into Kenya. ‎He also assured residents that the government was committed to protecting lives and property amid growing fears over stray ammunition. ‎ Kanja disclosed that two women, one Kenyan and another Ethiopian, had died after being struck by stray bullets, while several others had sustained injuries. ‎"One life has been lost on the Kenyan side after a woman was hit by a stray bullet on the neck. We have also recorded injuries arising from stray bullets. The best way to address this situation is to ensure the conflict is resolved quickly," he said. ‎The police chief also disclosed that approximately 10,000 displaced people were still living in temporary shelters and public institutions around Moyale, as humanitarian agencies continued providing emergency assistance. ‎The fighting has disrupted cross-border trade, movement of goods and services and electricity supply to Moyale, which relies heavily on power from Ethiopia. ‎The British advisory further maintains restrictions on several other parts of northern and eastern Kenya over terrorism threats, particularly from the Somalia-based al Shabaab militant group.‎ The FCDO advises against all travel to Mandera county, parts of Wajir county, most of Garissa county and parts of Lamu county. ‎It also advises against all but essential travel to Garissa Town, parts of Tana River county and sections of the coastline. ‎The latest warning adds to concerns over the security situation in the Horn of Africa, where instability across national borders continues to affect communities, trade and movement of people. ‎The FCDO said its travel advice is regularly reviewed as security conditions change, urging British nationals to consult its guidance before travelling. ‎The warning does not amount to a general travel ban on Kenya but specifically targets areas assessed to face heightened security risks. The report’s findings describe two sides of the same fiscal problem. The proliferation of government institutions, including an estimated 153 ministries across jurisdictions , stretches an already limited fiscal envelope. At the same time, the security sector, which absorbs the largest and most rigid share of public spending, is paying for soldiers who may not exist, may have deserted, or may be drawing salaries while serving elsewhere. The payroll gap is stark. The SNA payroll lists approximately 47,438 personnel , but a verification exercise through the army’s human resource management information system found only about 42,000 active troops . The gap of roughly 9,600 represents nearly one-fifth of the payroll, a significant share of the wage bill paid to inactive, unverified, or non-deployable personnel. The report notes that this gap has significant implications, including substantial fiscal leakage, reduced funding for operational readiness, and weak personnel management and accountability systems. Resolving these cases would generate recurrent savings, though not immediately, as exits carry transition costs, including lump-sum payments for deceased personnel and ongoing pension obligations for retirees. A History of Ghost Soldiers The problem is not new. A 2016 UN Monitoring Group report found that the SNA’s original lists of troops for payment often did not reflect reality on the ground, “indicating the historic prevalence of ghost soldiers, and consistent misappropriation of funds allocated for SNA salaries” . The report described three independent, incomplete, and likely incompatible databases of SNA troops eligible for stipends and salaries, with no single source of truth. The government has taken steps to address the problem. Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi said in April 2026 that the Ministry of Defence had made progress through a nationwide force census and biometric registration, through which the accurate number of personnel was verified and a credible national force registry was established. He said the ministry is moving toward a monthly personnel verification system directly linked to payroll and presence at duty stations and operational areas . But the World Bank’s data suggests the gap persists. The report calls for continuous biometric payroll verification, integrated with HRMIS and SFMIS, to establish a credible staffing baseline and eliminate unverified personnel. The 153 Ministries and the Cost of Proliferation The institutional proliferation is equally costly. The report notes that proposals for new agencies often originate from sector-level donor advice, supported by externally financed projects that also provide legislative drafting assistance. Without fully accounting for fiscal, capacity, and coordination constraints, this leads to “institutional proliferation rather than effective capacity expansion.” The World Bank’s reform scenario estimates that consolidating government structures, including reducing the number of FGS ministries from 25 to about 15 , could generate expenditure savings of approximately 0.4 percentage points of GDP . Those savings, combined with revenue gains, would make possible higher spending on education, infrastructure, and security. But the savings are not automatic. The report notes that Article 25 of the PFM Act requires draft legislation to include a statement of budgetary implications and to be reviewed by the Ministry of Finance before Cabinet and parliamentary consideration. This requirement is not consistently followed in practice. Critical Note The two findings are connected. A government that cannot control the size of its cabinet and the number of its agencies is unlikely to control the size of its army payroll. Both reflect a political economy in which institutions are created to reward allies, provide employment, and distribute resources, rather than to deliver services or security. The 153 ministries and the 9,600 unverified soldiers are not separate problems. They are symptoms of the same disease. The government’s biometric verification efforts are a step in the right direction. But the World Bank’s data suggests that the gap between the payroll and the active force remains large, and that the savings from closing it will be gradual and partially offset by transition costs. The 153 ministries, meanwhile, are not being consolidated at the pace the report recommends. The fiscal pressure is real, but the political will to address its root causes is not yet evident. For Somalia’s international partners, the implication is uncomfortable. The country’s security forces are being asked to assume greater responsibility as AU troops withdraw, but the payroll that sustains them is leaking resources to unverified personnel. The government’s commitment to reform is genuine, but the pace of reform is slower than the pace of the security transition. The gap between the two is where the risk lies. The men, identified as Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh, were accused of throwing petrol bombs and grenades, using firearms and bladed weapons, and setting fire to public facilities in Karaj, west of Tehran. Iran’s Tasnim news agency said the Supreme Court upheld their convictions for allegedly carrying out operations on behalf of Israel, the United States and hostile groups. The executions are the latest in a series of death sentences linked to the protests, which began in December over rising living costs before escalating into widespread demonstrations against the government. The unrest peaked on January 8 and 9, with Iranian authorities reporting more than 3,000 deaths and blaming the violence on what they described as terrorist acts backed by Washington and Tel Aviv. Foreign-based rights groups have reported higher death tolls, while accounts received by the BBC indicate that security forces opened fire on unarmed protesters. The number of executions in Iran has also increased since US and Israeli strikes on the country began in late February. Houthi media report 33 killed in Saudi air strikes in Yemen At least 33 people, including women and children, have been killed in air strikes in Yemen’s al-Shariyah district, east of Sanaa, according to media outlets affiliated with the Houthi movement. The Houthi-run Al Masirah television station broadcast footage of rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of damaged buildings and carrying injured people to nearby hospitals. The group’s Saba news agency said 39 people were injured in the attacks, which it blamed on Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia and the coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government had not commented on the reported strikes. The Saudi-led coalition has fought the Houthis for more than a decade, although hostilities had remained relatively subdued for several years before the conflict escalated again following the Iran war. The renewed fighting has included Houthi attacks on Saudi targets and vessels using the Red Sea as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz. The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced since hostilities resumed, while responsibility for a separate deadly market attack in Taiz province remains disputed. White House refuses to ease immigration crackdown after midterm losses Donald Trump, US President’s administration has vowed to continue its mass deportation campaign despite the Republican Party’s losses in last week’s midterm elections, rejecting suggestions that the results could prompt a change in immigration policy. The White House said the administration would not slow efforts to arrest and deport undocumented immigrants accused of criminal activity. The Department of Homeland Security also insisted that Immigration and Customs Enforcement would continue enforcing immigration laws under Trump’s leadership. The president’s decision to promote immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff had already signalled that the administration was unlikely to soften its approach. Exit polls showed immigration was the third most important issue for voters, behind the economy and the state of democracy. However, US officials told CBS, the BBC’s US partner, that the administration attributed its electoral losses mainly to concerns about the economy, the cost of living and the war with Iran rather than its immigration crackdown. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis maintained that Trump had been stronger on immigration enforcement than any previous president. Poland mourns six killed in Krakow shooting Poland has begun two days of national mourning after a gunman killed six people and wounded 16 others in a shooting in Krakow’s historic main square, prompting tighter security and renewed concern over extremist violence. The attack on Saturday left the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man, and two police officers among those injured. The suspect remains in critical condition in hospital, according to local authorities, while the government said the shooting may have been inspired by far-right ideology. The incident has shaken public confidence in a country often regarded as safer than many of its Western European neighbours. It also follows school stabbings in October that officials linked to inflammatory material circulating online. Opposition nationalist politicians have questioned the government’s suggestion of a far-right motive, challenging the evidence behind the claim. Investigators are continuing to establish the circumstances of the attack, which took place in Krakow’s UNESCO-listed old town, a major tourist destination. Eisenkot seeks broad Israeli government as Netanyahu’s path to power remains uncertain Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli military chief, has pledged to form a broad government after President Isaac Herzog gave him the mandate to try to build a coalition following last month’s inconclusive election. Herzog formally handed Eisenkot the task on Sunday, making him the first candidate to attempt to form a government after the October 27 vote left both his camp and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc short of a parliamentary majority. Eisenkot described the negotiations as extraordinarily complex and called for a national emergency government. He said Israel was approaching a critical point and needed new leadership capable of addressing security and political challenges. Herzog highlighted the threat from Iran, the need to advance peace efforts in Gaza and negotiations with Lebanon and other neighbouring countries. Eisenkot could seek support from Arab parties, negotiate with ultra-Orthodox factions or attempt a unity government with Netanyahu. However, each option faces significant political obstacles, making his chances of securing a majority uncertain. AFRICA Seven killed, more than 100 injured in train collision near Egypt’s Giza At least seven people have been killed and more than 100 injured after two passenger trains collided near Giza, south of Egypt’s capital Cairo, causing several carriages to derail. Egypt’s railway authority said one train travelling from Giza to Fayoum struck the rear of another service heading from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks. Several carriages overturned and fell down an embankment, prompting a large emergency response. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered authorities to investigate the accident and hold anyone found negligent accountable. The public prosecutor’s office warned that the death toll could rise as rescue and recovery operations continued. Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, the Health Minister said hospitals in the area had been placed on high alert, with injured passengers receiving treatment for fractures and head injuries. The Egyptian Red Crescent also deployed teams to provide assistance and psychological support to victims and their families. ANC suffers worst-ever local election result in South Africa South Africa’s African National Congress has recorded its worst performance in local government elections since the end of apartheid, securing 30.76 percent of the national vote and suffering major losses across provinces and cities. The result marks a sharp decline from the 46 percent the party won in 2021 and the 64.82 percent recorded two decades ago. The ANC retained a majority in only one of the country’s nine provinces, Limpopo, compared with six in the previous local elections, and secured the most votes in just two of the eight major cities. The Democratic Alliance came second with 24.64 percent, retaining control of Cape Town, while former president Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe party won 9.76 percent and emerged as the leading party in Durban. The Economic Freedom Fighters secured 6.22 per cent, placing fourth. Fikile Mbalula, ANC secretary-general described the outcome as catastrophic, citing the high cost of living and growing discontent among middle-class voters. President Cyril Ramaphosa said the party accepted the electorate’s verdict, as the result deepens pressure on the ANC following its loss of a parliamentary majority in the 2024 national elections. Somalia’s Supreme Court rejects president’s term extension Somalia’s Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his tenure, escalating a political confrontation between the presidency and judiciary over the country’s electoral process. The court said constitutional changes approved by parliament in March could not be applied retrospectively to extend Mohamud’s current term, which expired in May. The administration had added a year to his four-year mandate, a move opposition groups condemned as an attempt to prolong his stay in power. The ruling also declared the dismissal of Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed null and void, saying the president lacked the authority to remove him outside established constitutional procedures. Mohamud had appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, a former chief justice, as Ahmed’s replacement, arguing that the decision followed complaints about the administration of justice. The court ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting the government’s plans for nationwide polls next year. Mohamud says his proposed reforms are intended to replace Somalia’s clan-based electoral system with direct democratic elections, which the country has not held nationwide since 1969. Kenyan court sentences doomsday cult leader to 200 years for 191 deaths A Kenyan court has sentenced doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the deaths of 191 people, most of them children, in one of the country’s deadliest cases of cult-related killings. Mackenzie and 28 others were convicted after prosecutors established that he instructed members of his religious group to starve their children and themselves to death in the belief that they would meet Jesus. Judge Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore primary responsibility for directing the fasting and that the sentence was intended to reflect the gravity of the crimes. The court imposed 100 years for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation. The sentences in each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years. Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near Kenya’s coast. Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, but the judge declined to impose it, saying imprisonment preserved the possibility of rehabilitation. Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies. Egypt reopens embassy in Libya’s Tripoli after 12 years Egypt has reopened its embassy in Libya’s capital, Tripoli, after a 12-year closure, signalling closer engagement with the country’s western-based administration and a shift in Cairo’s diplomatic approach. Egypt’s foreign ministry announced the reopening on Saturday, with Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty attending the ceremony. He said the embassy’s historical significance reflected the longstanding cultural and human ties between the two countries. The move marks a change for Cairo, which has been a prominent supporter of eastern-based military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose forces and political allies rival the internationally recognised Government of National Unity in Tripoli. Egypt closed its embassy in 2014 as fighting intensified and rival administrations emerged in the country’s east and west. Libya has remained divided since the 2011 uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi, with competing political and military authorities exercising control over different parts of the country. The reopening could strengthen Egypt’s diplomatic engagement with the Tripoli administration as efforts to resolve Libya’s political divisions continue. Somalia currently contends with low electrification rates, exceptionally high electricity tariffs, and a systemic reliance on imported fossil fuels to operate local diesel generators. Despite the country possessing substantial natural resources, particularly high equatorial solar irradiance and favorable coastal wind regimes, the integration of these sustainable energy alternatives into the broader national network remains constrained. To investigate the practical potential of transitioning away from fossil fuel dependence, researchers conducted a systematic review examining peer-reviewed literature, policy documents, and empirical case studies published between 2010 and 2025. The investigation synthesizes technical performance metrics, capital requirements, operating expenses, and institutional structures into an integrated analytical framework to assess how hybrid configurations can sustainably meet burgeoning power demand across urban, rural, and off-grid districts. The study contextualizes Somalia’s immediate electrification challenge within its broader demographic trajectory and national development priorities. Driven by steady economic growth and population expansion, Somalia faces a rapidly escalating demand for power that will require domestic generation capacity to double within the coming decade. Historical data shows that production capacity expanded from 115 megawatts to 344 megawatts between June 2015 and June 2021, and household survey data from 2023 indicated that over half the population had gained access to electricity services. Nevertheless, roughly 1.3 billion individuals globally lack reliable electricity, and sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected, with sixty-eight percent of its 915 million residents deficient in electricity access. For Somalia, relying on decentralized diesel generators exposes the economy to volatile international oil markets, highlighting the strategic necessity of harnessing local, clean energy alternatives. To establish the technical foundation for hybrid renewable deployment, the research outlines the physical and complementary dynamics of combining solar photovoltaic arrays with wind turbines. The analytical modeling evaluated solar resources characterized by an average daily irradiation of 5.5 kilowatt-hours per square meter alongside average wind speeds ranging between 4 and 6 meters per second across representative territory. Photovoltaic conversion utilizes semiconductor materials operating on the photovoltaic effect, delivering average system conversion efficiencies between fifteen and twenty percent. Determining the optimal system dimensions requires precise mathematical formulations to balance electrical generation against load demands while minimizing total lifecycle expenditure. The study models the sizing of solar photovoltaic capacity by dividing the daily electrical energy demand by the product of average solar irradiance and array efficiency, incorporating derating factors to account for temperature coefficients, module operating temperatures, and wiring losses. The required number of solar panels is subsequently determined by dividing this total rated capacity by the nominal peak power rating of an individual commercial panel. Wind turbine sizing relies on stochastic modeling that accounts for temporal velocity distributions rather than simple average speeds, calculating turbine numbers by dividing aggregate required wind capacity by single turbine outputs. Backup diesel generation capacity is mathematically specified to match or exceed the peak electrical load, ensuring that critical demand is consistently satisfied during protracted intervals of overcast skies, calm winds, or extreme consumption spikes. Energy storage and power conditioning architectures represent critical components in maintaining electrical reliability and supply autonomy within autonomous hybrid networks. The research details sizing protocols for battery storage banks based on daily load consumption, designated days of autonomy, and predefined depth of discharge parameters to prevent premature cell degradation. Lead-acid batteries provide an affordable upfront solution with an established recycling infrastructure but require operating limits around fifty percent depth of discharge and frequent physical maintenance. In contrast, modern lithium-ion batteries support depths of discharge reaching eighty percent, presenting longer cycle lifetimes, superior energy density, and reduced servicing requirements, with emerging flow batteries offering future utility-scale opportunities. Power conversion apparatus must be meticulously balanced; inverters converting direct current to alternating current are sized between twenty-five and thirty percent above total appliance wattage and three times the rating of inductive compressor loads, while active power requirements for battery recharging are modeled as functions of daily insolation and array productivity. System performance and multi-scenario optimization were evaluated using the HOMER Pro simulation software developed by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The simulation engine models hourly power balance constraints across an entire operational year, continuously comparing load requirements against synthetic Typical Meteorological Year weather sequences. When solar array output exceeds demand, power is prioritized for direct consumption with excess directed toward battery charging. During cloudy intervals or periods of weak insolation, battery state of charge is monitored, releasing stored energy until reaching the maximum depth of discharge threshold, at which point backup diesel generation automatically engages to bridge the deficit. Historical cost trends analyzed from 2010 through 2025 illustrate dramatic reductions in renewable technology capital expenditures, fundamentally shifting the economic landscape in favor of hybrid adoption. Over the same timeframe, the cost of operating conventional diesel generators remained elevated and is projected to rise further due to increasing fuel logistics expenses and carbon compliance standards. Empirical results from a localized district feasibility study demonstrate that a properly configured hybrid system can reliably serve an electrical demand of approximately 2.5 megawatts with an anticipated five percent annual load growth. The financial modeling indicates that while hybrid renewable installations require substantial initial capital investment compared to buying simple diesel generators, their drastically lower fuel and maintenance costs result in a markedly lower Levelized Cost of Electricity over the equipment lifespan. The estimated payback period for capital recovery ranges between three and seven years, dictated by local financing terms, system sizing ratios, and load factors. In addition to delivering cheaper electricity over time, deploying hybrid microgrids provides significant environmental dividends by displacing fossil fuel combustion, abating local atmospheric pollutants, cutting greenhouse gas emissions, and insulating local businesses from international fossil fuel price shocks. Despite the unequivocal technical viability and long-term economic advantages, the review identifies critical structural barriers that currently impede large-scale commercial renewable deployment across Somalia. To overcome these developmental bottlenecks, the study outlines a structured strategic roadmap designed to accelerate clean energy adoption and guide policymaking across Somalia and comparable developing regions. Engaging local municipalities, community leaders, and domestic firms ensures that system designs match real-world load demand while cultivating local workforce capabilities through job creation in installation, system servicing, and continuous performance monitoring. By implementing these coordinated technical, financial, and policy interventions, Somalia can harness its abundant solar and wind resources to establish a resilient, self-sustaining energy foundation. The pavilion was inaugurated by Somalia’s Minister of Commerce and Industry, Jama Mohamed Hassan, alongside Somalia’s Ambassador to China, Dr. Hodan Osman Abdi, during the ninth edition of the international trade exhibition. advertisements The ceremony was attended by senior Somali government officials, representatives of the Somali Chamber of Commerce and Industry, business leaders and members of the Somali delegation. Somali companies are displaying products including sesame seeds, frankincense and myrrh, while promoting investment opportunities in livestock, fisheries and mineral resources. The government hopes the exhibition will help Somali producers establish direct connections with Chinese importers, identify market requirements and secure new commercial partnerships. The expo, held at Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center from Nov. 5 to 10, has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors and participants from 162 countries, regions and international organizations, according to organizers. Somalia is among the countries participating in the expo’s national exhibition for the first time, providing a platform to introduce its products and investment potential to international buyers. The Somali Embassy in China said the initiative was intended to help domestic businesses understand Chinese market demands, improve product quality and develop commercial relationships that could lead to long-term export agreements. The exhibition also provides an opportunity to attract investment in local production, processing and packaging, which could enable Somali businesses to export more finished products rather than relying primarily on raw materials. “The Embassy of Somalia in China views this participation as a significant starting point for expanding the country’s exports and creating new markets that will benefit Somali farmers, livestock herders, fishers, and businesspeople,” the embassy said. The embassy credited the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the Office of the Prime Minister, other government institutions and Somali entrepreneurs for coordinating the country's participation. It also praised Somali businesspeople based in China and those who traveled from Somalia for presenting products and investment opportunities at the pavilion. The embassy said it would continue facilitating connections between Somali and Chinese businesses and following up on commercial opportunities identified during the exhibition. Somalia’s participation comes as the government seeks to diversify export markets, attract foreign investment and strengthen the country's domestic production capacity. The first 109 soldiers left at the end of last month, and all 4,500 currently deployed will permanently return to Uganda by the end of 2027. “Things are not dire now,” said Ali Omar, ​Somalia’s foreign affairs minister. Since then, Ugandan forces have been key players in fighting alongside the Somali National Army to “recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations”. More recently they have also been a part of the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which “focused on strengthening Somalia’s security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country’s security”. But the future of Aussom has been “thrown into doubt” after US authorities decided to cancel funding for a UN logistics office, which is integral to the operation, said Deutsche Welle . Washington is the coalition’s largest donor. It has “voiced frustration with a lack of progress in the fight against Al-Shabab”, and accused the Somali government of “failing to unite the country and implement political reforms”. This coincided with last month’s closure of the UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia after more than “three decades of peace-building”. Preventing a ‘security vacuum’ African Union peacekeepers are planning to move from Barawe, 135 miles southwest of the capital Mogadishu, to replace the outgoing Ugandan troops. They will move to four bases – Sabid-Anole, Bariire, Awdheegle and Bulonagad – which are deemed “critical” to protecting Mogadishu, said The Associated Press . Failure to do so would allow Al Shabab to exploit the “security vacuum” left behind. This turning point marks a “significant development in Somalia’s ongoing security transition”, said the Somali Guardian . Barawe is a “strategically important coastal town and port” and Shalanbood, another facility vacated by Ugandan forces, is a “key settlement along a major transport corridor” in Lower Shabelle, a region where Al Shabab has maintained a "significant presence”. It also comes at a “politically sensitive juncture”. Political divisions and differing priorities among groups within government “risk diverting attention and resources from military operations and the broader campaign against insurgency”. This is not a “routine change of command”, it is a “test” of the Somali National Army’s “preparedness to assume a greater share of the country’s security responsibilities”. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Abdullah Bozkurt/Stockholm Turkey is developing a sprawling rocket launch facility on Somalia’s Indian Ocean coast that is publicly presented as a civilian spaceport for commercial satellite launches but is also emerging as a potential testing ground for the country’s expanding long-range ballistic missile arsenal, according to Turkish government documents, parliamentary testimony and reports on Ankara’s enhanced military hardware acquisition plans. An examination of financial records published by the Turkish Space Agency (Türkiye Uzay Ajansı, TUA) reveals that the government allocated 2.1 billion Turkish lira, equivalent to approximately $42 million at November 2026 exchange rates, for transfer to the Defense Industry Support Fund under the country’s national space access and spaceport program. The financial arrangement, disclosed in a footnote to the agency’s 2026 performance program, establishes an official connection between Turkey’s civilian space ambitions and the financial mechanism used to support its military and its defense industry. The documents do not specify how much of the allocation, if any, has been spent on the construction of the Somali facility or on missile-related infrastructure. The project, estimated in media reports to cost approximately $350 million, is taking shape near the coastal town of Warsheikh, about 70 kilometers north of Mogadishu. The planned development covers an area reportedly measuring about 900 square kilometers, giving Turkey access to a substantial stretch of territory for launching rockets toward the Indian Ocean. Its location is critical to both the civilian and potential military dimensions of the project. Somalia’s proximity to the equator offers advantages for putting satellites into orbit, while the vast expanse of the Indian Ocean provides a geographically convenient corridor for long-range missile trials, reducing the risk of rocket debris falling on densely populated areas or neighboring countries. The clearest documentary indication of the project’s connection to the Turkish military appears in TUA’s official 2026 Performance Program, published on the agency’s website. The detail was buried in a footnote on page 23 that said an additional 2.1 billion lira was incorporated into the agency’s 2025 budget under the National Space Program’s Uzaya Erişim ve Uzay Limanı (Access to Space and Spaceport) activity. The Turkish Space Agency’s 2026 Performance Program reveals a 2.1 billion lira ($42 million) allocation for transfer to the Defense Industry Support Fund under its spaceport program, highlighting a financial link between Turkey’s civilian space ambitions and its defense industry: The document specifies that the allocation was intended for transfer to the Savunma Sanayii Destekleme Fonu (Defense Industry Support Fund, SSDF), citing legislation published in the Official Gazette on July 24, 2025, issue No. 32965. The fund is a vital financing instrument for Turkey’s military-industrial programs and is institutionally distinct from the Turkish Armed Forces’ operational budget. It supports the development and procurement of defense technologies, including strategically significant domestic capabilities. The use of this financing mechanism for a program publicly promoted around satellite launches raises questions about the division of responsibilities between TUA and Turkey’s defense establishment, particularly the Presidency of the Defense Industry (SSB) which reports directly to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. The same performance program puts TUA’s overall 2025 budget at approximately 4.58 billion lira, with a 2026 budget of 5.92 billion lira. In his introduction to the program, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said the planned spaceport was intended to support Turkey’s independent access to space and strategic launches. The description reinforces the government’s emphasis on strategic autonomy, without defining the military or civilian status of individual future launches. The connection between Turkey’s space ambitions and its military-industrial establishment predates the construction of the Somali facility. TUA’s 2022 Activity Report reveals that the agency began an extensive assessment in 2021 under the National Space Program to study future launch vehicles, payloads, orbital requirements and rocket launch facilities. Four working groups were established to examine payloads, launch vehicles, innovative propulsion and component technologies and launch-base infrastructure. On February 22, 2022, TUA held a meeting to present the findings of its Independent Access to Space and Spaceport Analysis Report. Among the organizations invited were leading Turkish defense contractors Roketsan, ASELSAN, Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ/TAI), STM and DeltaV, together with TÜBİTAK SAGE, TÜBİTAK UZAY, TÜRKSAT and other aerospace companies. The agency said the resulting analysis was distributed to relevant stakeholders. It was kept confidential from public scrutiny. Turkey’s GÖKTÜRK-2, a domestically developed Earth observation and reconnaissance satellite designed to provide high-resolution imagery for civilian and military applications, is launched into orbit aboard a Chinese Long March rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China on December 18, 2012. The involvement of Roketsan is particularly significant. The company is a major developer of Turkish rocket and missile systems, including the Tayfun ballistic missile family. It also works on technologies intended to provide Turkey with independent satellite-launch capabilities. TUA’s website identifies Roketsan as the contractor selected under a 2018 agreement with the Presidency of the Defense Industry for the Micro Satellite Launch System, known by its Turkish abbreviation MUFS. The program aims to develop the ability to put satellites weighing up to 100 kilograms into low Earth orbit at altitudes of at least 400 kilometers. It also envisages the development of domestic infrastructure for manufacturing, testing and launching space vehicles. Although satellite-launch vehicles and ballistic missiles serve different purposes, some of their underlying technologies overlap, particularly rocket propulsion, structural materials, guidance and control and testing infrastructure. The overlap means that investment in satellite-launch technology can also strengthen the industrial capabilities needed for sophisticated missile systems. Further evidence of the facility’s anticipated use by Turkish defense contractors emerged in December 2025 when Selçuk Bayraktar, chairman of drone manufacturer Baykar and son-in-law of President Erdogan, discussed the Somali project at a technology event in Istanbul. Bayraktar said the state had begun construction of the launch facility and specifically identified Roketsan as a prospective user. He also said he hoped to use the site for launch vehicles developed by his own aerospace ventures. His remarks identified a direct prospective role for Roketsan at the Somali facility, going beyond its participation in the earlier feasibility studies. Turkey’s then-defense minister Hulusi Akar examines the İMECE satellite, the country’s first domestically developed high-resolution Earth observation satellite, during a visit on June 4, 2020, as officials completed the assembly of its final components ahead of testing. The satellite was designed for civilian and military reconnaissance applications. Turkey’s search for an overseas launch facility is closely connected to the geographical limitations it faces in developing both an independent space program and longer-range missiles. Launching spacecraft eastward from a location close to the equator can improve the efficiency of reaching certain orbits by taking advantage of the Earth’s rotation. Such launches also require large safety zones to accommodate the possibility of falling rocket components. Turkey’s own geography creates complications. To its north lies the Black Sea, bordered by Russia, Ukraine and other countries, while its southern approaches involve the Mediterranean, Cyprus and densely trafficked air and maritime routes. A launch site facing the Indian Ocean offers a potentially much larger testing corridor. President Erdogan had previously announced plans to increase Turkey’s inventory of missiles with ranges of around 800 kilometers while accelerating work on systems capable of reaching 2,000 kilometers. Reports suggested that Turkey is working on testing missiles with a range of some 6,000 kilometers as well. The Somali site could provide testing opportunities for those programs, although there is no publicly established evidence that particular missile systems have been assigned to launches from Warsheikh. According to an account published by the state-run Anadolu news agency on January 1, 2026, the Somali project is being developed in three phases, with the initial focus on establishing launch infrastructure and the subsequent ambition of offering commercial services. The envisioned facility would initially support Turkish satellites and eventually serve foreign customers seeking access to low Earth orbit and other orbital destinations. The government also expects the project to stimulate the development of domestic rocket engines, propulsion technologies, advanced materials, avionics and ground-support systems. Such programs routinely involve technologies relevant to military communications, reconnaissance and navigation, even when launch services are sold commercially. Turkey is believed to have been trying to combine its expanding ballistic missile ambitions under the pretext of developing a spaceport in Somalia. Ankara has not publicly disclosed a comprehensive operational framework separating the site’s civilian satellite-launch activities from any military testing arrangements. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan meets with Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud at the Presidential Dolmabahçe Office in Istanbul on April 16, 2026. The government provided a fresh confirmation of the project’s progress during a November 2, 2026, hearing of the Turkish Parliament’s Planning and Budget Committee. Presenting the Industry and Technology Ministry’s 2027 budget, Minister Kacır said the government was moving toward the capability to launch Turkish satellites using domestically developed rockets. He specifically referred to construction of the Somali spaceport as a central element of this ambition. The minister said the facility would give Turkey independent access to space and enable it to obtain a larger share of the global space economy. He carefully avoided making any reference to the military aspect of the project. His remarks nevertheless confirmed that the Somali facility has advanced beyond an initial proposal and forms part of Turkey’s active national space strategy. The Turkish government also has ambitions to deploy space-based systems that could support intelligence collection, communications and navigation, capabilities of obvious interest to the country’s military establishment. Another potentially important development appears in a June 26, 2026, announcement published by TUA. The agency disclosed that it had hosted a meeting involving the ambassadors of Somalia and Qatar in Ankara to discuss cooperation in space-related activities. The Somali ambassador, Fathudin Ali Mohamed, and Qatari Ambassador Faisal bin Abdulla Al-Henzab attended the meeting, which focused on access to space, space systems, opportunities for cooperation and regional partnerships. According to the agency, participants also considered ways to strengthen exchanges of knowledge, experience and technology. Personnel from the Somali National Army’s 5th Eagle Battalion participate in infiltration training conducted by Turkey’s 1st Airborne and Commando Brigade Command, as announced by the Turkish Ministry of Defense on October 16, 2026. The exercise highlights Turkey’s continuing role in training and strengthening Somalia’s military forces. Although the announcement did not specifically identify the Somali launch complex as the subject of a trilateral agreement, the presence of both countries at a meeting devoted to space access is noteworthy. Qatar is an important strategic partner of Erdogan’s government, with extensive defense and economic ties to Turkey, including defense-industry cooperation. While Turkey provides muscle and technology to military projects, Qatar is poised to bankroll such ambitious projects in Turkey. The spaceport is being established against the background of Turkey’s extensive military, economic and political involvement in Somalia. Ankara has substantially expanded its presence in the country since Erdogan’s visit to Mogadishu in 2011, building relationships across defense cooperation, infrastructure, energy, education and government institutions. Turkey opened a major overseas military training facility in Mogadishu in 2017. Commonly known as TURKSOM, the installation serves as a center for training Somali military personnel and represents one of Turkey’s most important military commitments outside its immediate region. The facility, reportedly established at a cost of around $50 million, has the capacity to train thousands of Somali soldiers. Turkey and Somalia have subsequently concluded additional defense and maritime security agreements, expanding Ankara’s role in helping protect Somali territorial waters and supporting Somali security institutions.In July 2024 the Turkish Parliament approved a presidential motion authorizing the deployment of Turkish naval forces to Somalia under the countries’ defense cooperation arrangements. Turkey’s expanding security role has coincided with growing commercial interests, including infrastructure management and prospective hydrocarbon exploration. Turkish companies have a significant presence in the management of Mogadishu’s airport and seaport, while Ankara has also pursued agreements involving offshore and onshore energy exploration. The spaceport would add another strategically important installation to this network, potentially allowing Turkey to combine military training, maritime security, aerospace technology and launch operations within a single partner country. The financial structure of the project remains largely undisclosed. Although TUA’s performance program identifies a 2.1 billion lira allocation associated with a transfer to the Defense Industry Support Fund, the agency has not established in the reviewed documents which contracts were financed through that mechanism or whether the money was spent directly on the Warsheikh site. Similarly, the frequently reported $350 million construction estimate has not been reconciled with a publicly available, comprehensive project budget. There are also unanswered questions about the companies responsible for building the complex. Turkey’s ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, and TURKSOM military base commander Maj. Gen. Sabahattin Kalkan, accompanied by a Turkish delegation, visit Warsheikh in Somalia’s Middle Shabelle region to inspect the site of a Turkish-developed satellite launch facility. The October 5, 2026, visit comes amid Ankara’s expanding military and commercial presence in Somalia, including plans for a new port, special economic zone and industrial facilities near Warsheikh. Turkey’s Albayrak Group, a conglomerate with considerable business interests in Somalia and close ties to President Erdogan, has been mentioned in reports concerning visits by Turkish delegations to the spaceport construction site. Ahmet Sami İşler, the group’s general manager in Somalia and chairman of the Turkey–Somalia Business Council, reportedly briefed a visiting delegation on the project. The Albayrak Group has longstanding ties to Erdogan’s government and has supported political Islamist initiatives in Turkey and abroad. Its flagship media outlet, the Islamist Yeni Şafak daily, has been a staunch supporter of Erdogan and his political Islamist agenda, consistently promoting his government’s policies and ideological positions. The government’s own statements more clearly identify Roketsan as a prospective user of the facility, while TUA’s earlier planning documents show the involvement of numerous other Turkish defense and aerospace organizations. Satellite launch vehicles and ballistic missiles rely on some common engineering disciplines, including propulsion, aerodynamics, structural design, navigation and control. Investment in one field can therefore provide technical benefits to the other. The involvement of the Presidency of the Defense Industry and companies such as Roketsan reinforces the strategic importance of this technological convergence. The Erdogan government has consistently promoted domestic defense production and technological independence as central pillars of Turkey’s national security strategy. The Somali spaceport appears to fit into this broader strategy, combining ambitions to compete in the international space industry with the development of strategically sensitive technologies. For now, however, it remains unclear how much of the facility’s infrastructure, financing and operational capacity will ultimately be devoted to advancing Turkey’s military missile program. football.summary: كثف منتخب السودان استعداداته لمواجهتي السنغال الحاسمتين، المقررتين في 12 و16 نوفمبر، ضمن تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية 2027. يأتي ذلك بعد أن انضم نجوم الهلال والمريخ إلى التدريبات في كيغالي، بعد غيابهم عن الحصة التدريبية الأولى التي اقتصرت على المحترفين واللاعبين الشباب. يضم المنتخب 19 لاعبًا من الفريقين، مما يعكس قوة التشكيلة الأساسية. من جهة أخرى، طمأن الطاقم الطبي الجماهير بشأن حالة حارس المرمى فريد مصطفى، الذي تعرض لوعكة صحية استدعت نقله للمستشفى، حيث أكد الطبيب محمد النعيم أنه سيستأنف تدريباته بعد فترة راحة قصيرة. يهدف المنتخب السوداني لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في المباراتين لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل للنهائيات. سيخوض الفريق ثلاث حصص تدريبية قبل مغادرته إلى داكار في 9 نوفمبر.
